headline: Zoo Lions Fed Whole Carcasses Start Acting Wild Again
meta_description: Australian researchers found that feeding zoo lions whole carcasses on a feast-and-fast schedule triggers natural wild behaviors and eating patterns.
summary_short: When Adelaide University scientists gave zoo lions whole carcasses every nine days, the animals began eating three times longer and displaying wild-like behavior pattern…
body:
Researchers at Adelaide University and Monarto Safari Park have discovered that zoo lions behave dramatically more like their wild cousins when fed whole animal carcasses on a feast-and-fast schedule. Over three months of continuous video monitoring, three adult male African lions receiving approximately 200 kilograms of carcasses every nine days spent nearly three times longer eating, engaged in natural tearing and manipulating of food, and rested heavily after meals before gradually increasing activity during fasting periods. This cycling matched the rhythms documented in wild lion populations—a stark contrast to the predictable daily feeding routines most captive lions experience.

Lead researcher Lesia Hryhorenko explained the significance: wild lions don't eat on schedule. They experience natural periods of feast and famine depending on hunting success. By introducing whole carcasses that remained available for up to three days, researchers gave the lions opportunity to perform authentic feeding behaviors—tearing, pulling, and manipulating food over extended periods—that are central to their wild ecology but impossible with processed meals.

A surprising finding emerged around pacing, a repetitive behavior often assumed to signal hunger or distress. Pacing increased slightly but not consistently as fasting periods lengthened. Instead, the largest increases occurred around predictable events like keeper arrivals, suggesting pacing linked more to routine anticipation than actual hunger. Importantly, whole carcass feeding caused no increase in aggression or social disruption among the lions.

Associate Professor Alexandra Whittaker emphasized the broader lesson: animal behavior studies must track complete feeding cycles, not just immediate responses to food. What happens for days afterward matters. These findings open doors to better understanding how feeding practices affect captive carnivore welfare—and suggest that mimicking natural patterns might be one key to keeping zoo animals mentally and physically healthier.
quick_facts: Adelaide University researchers studied three male lions at Monarto Safari Park
Lions ate three times longer when given whole carcasses every nine days
Eight infrared cameras recorded 24-hour behavioral data over three months
Pacing linked to routine events, not hunger levels during fasting periods
Results published in Applied Animal Behaviour Science, October 2026
